lessons.title: Forces as vectors

steps.headline: A slanted force acts as a sideways part and an upward part.

lead.text: A force at an angle pushes across and up at once. Those two parts, at right angles, are its components. Together they act exactly as the force does.
For a force F at angle θ above the horizontal: across = F cos θ, up = F sin θ.
A free-body diagram shows only the forces acting on one isolated body.
The force below acts at 30° above the horizontal. Put your calculator in degrees.

reveal.text: You used the cosine because the horizontal side touches the angle: 10 cos 30° = 8.66 kN across. The vertical part, 10 sin 30°, is 5.00 kN.

steps.headline: Split 20 kN at 60° above the horizontal into its two components.

workedSteps.text: The horizontal side touches the angle, so use cosine.
The vertical side is opposite the angle, so use sine.
Check: the parts combine back to the original force.

steps.headline: A 5 kN cable pull runs along a line that rises 3 m for every 4 m across. Find its vertical component.

lead.text: Drawings often give a slope, not an angle. A slope of 3 in 4 is a right-angled triangle with sides 3 and 4. Pythagoras gives its long side, and the sine and cosine are just ratios of sides.

workedSteps.text: Find the long side of the slope triangle.
The vertical share is the rise over the long side.
Multiply the pull by that share, in kN.

steps.headline: Forces at right angles combine to a resultant found by Pythagoras.

lead.text: The single force that does the work of several is their resultant. Forces on one line simply add. At right angles their sizes do not add: square each, add, then take the root.
R = √(Rx² + Ry²)

reveal.text: Rx = 3 kN and Ry = 4 kN, so the resultant is √(9 + 16) = 5 kN. Adding the sizes would only be right for forces on one line.

lead.text: A point is in equilibrium when ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0. Drawn tip to tail, its forces then close into a polygon with no gap. Press Play to slide the arrows.

reveal.text: The third force must match the resultant of the other two in size and point exactly opposite it.

lessons.orientation: Resolve forces into components and add them on a free-body diagram.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two people pull a trolley along a straight rail. One pulls with 3 kN, the other with 4 kN, both the same way.

intro.promise: By the end you'll split a slanted force into two straight parts and combine forces at right angles.

recap.keyIdea: A slanted force acts as a horizontal part and a vertical part, and forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras, not by adding their sizes.

blocks.text: You split 10 kN at 30° into 8.66 kN across and 5.00 kN up, and found that a 5 kN pull on a 3 in 4 slope has a 3 kN vertical part.
Then you combined 3 kN and 4 kN at right angles into 5 kN, not 7 kN.

lessons.title: Turning effect: moments

steps.headline: A moment is a force times its perpendicular distance from the pivot.

lead.text: A moment measures how hard a force turns a body about a point. The distance counts at right angles from that point to the line the force acts along. Anticlockwise moments are positive here.
M = F × d
A spanner turns a bolt. The push is at right angles to the handle.

reveal.text: You multiplied the push by the full distance because it is at right angles: 150 × 0.3 = 45 N·m.

steps.headline: A 90 N push acts at 30° to a spanner, 0.4 m from the bolt. Find the moment about the bolt.

workedSteps.text: Only the part of the push across the spanner turns it.
Multiply by the full distance along the spanner.

steps.headline: The 150 N push is now at 30° to the spanner, still 0.3 m from the bolt. Find the moment.

workedSteps.text: Take the part of the push across the spanner.
Multiply that part by the 0.3 m distance, in N·m.

lead.text: Sketch the line the force acts along, then find its perpendicular distance from the bolt.

reveal.text: You found that the line of action runs through the bolt, so there is no perpendicular distance. That is why unknown forces are placed at the point you take moments about.

lead.text: A body at rest on a pivot has zero net moment. Add the moments with their signs: anticlockwise positive, clockwise negative. The sizes of the forces alone do not decide the balance.

reveal.text: The 300 N child turns the see-saw anticlockwise with 600 N·m, so a 400 N child must supply the same clockwise: 600 ÷ 400 metres.

lessons.orientation: Find the moment of a force about a point and balance clockwise against anticlockwise.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two children sit on a see-saw, each 2 m from the middle. The see-saw balances. One child weighs 300 N.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find how hard a force turns a body about a point, and use it to balance a beam.

recap.keyIdea: A moment is force times perpendicular distance from the pivot, and a body at rest has moments that cancel.

blocks.text: You found that a 150 N push at right angles gives 45 N·m at a bolt 0.3 m away. Tilted to 30° it gives only 22.5 N·m.
You balanced a see-saw by making a 300 N child's 600 N·m equal a 400 N child's, at 1.5 m.

lessons.title: Reactions of a supported beam

steps.headline: Take moments about a support and its own reaction drops out.

lead.text: A support pushes back on a beam with a reaction. A roller pushes only at right angles to its surface and lets the beam slide and turn. For a beam at rest, the forces and the moments both sum to zero.
The load sits nearer A than B, so A carries the larger share. Take moments about A.

reveal.text: About A the load turns the beam one way and the reaction at B the other. Balancing them gave 6 × RB = 12 × 2, so RB = 4 kN.

steps.headline: A 6 m beam on supports at x = 0 and x = 6 m carries 18 kN at x = 1 m. Find both reactions.

workedSteps.text: Take moments about A. The reaction at A passes through A, so it has no moment.
The two reactions must carry the whole load.

steps.headline: The 12 kN load is at x = 2 m on the 6 m beam, and RB is 4 kN. Find the reaction at A.

workedSteps.text: The two reactions must carry the whole load.
Subtract the reaction at B, in kN.

steps.headline: For reactions, a spread load acts as its total at the middle of its length.

lead.text: A load of w kN/m over a length L totals w × L. For finding reactions it can be replaced by that one force, acting at the middle of the loaded length. Inside the loaded length the bending is different.
Replace the spread load by one force first. Then take moments about the left support.

reveal.text: The spread load became one 12 kN force at 1.5 m, so moments about the left support gave the right-hand reaction. The same total spread evenly would give 6 kN each.

lead.text: A load beyond a support can swing the beam about it, so the far support has to pull down. Count upward as positive and keep the sign.

reveal.text: You kept the sign: the left support holds the beam down. A support built only to push would let that end lift off.

lessons.orientation: Use ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0 to find the support reactions of a beam.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A 6 m plank is held up by a post at each end. A 12 kN crate sits exactly halfway along it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the reactions at the two supports of a beam by taking moments, including spread loads and overhangs.

recap.keyIdea: Take moments about one support and its reaction drops out, which gives the other reaction. Vertical equilibrium then gives the first.

blocks.text: You found that a 12 kN load 2 m from A puts 4 kN on B and 8 kN on A, then replaced a 4 kN/m load over 3 m by one 12 kN force.
You also saw a load on an overhang pull the far support down, giving −5 kN at A.

recap.nextHook: Now take a truss, a frame of straight bars. How do you find the force in each bar?

lessons.title: Trusses: the method of joints

steps.headline: Each truss member carries a pure push or pull, and you find it one joint at a time.

lead.text: A truss is a frame of straight members pinned at joints and loaded only at joints. So each member is pulled (tension) or pushed (compression) along its length. The method of joints isolates one joint and balances the forces on it.
Isolate the apex joint, C. The two sloping members push on it equally, and their vertical parts together must hold up the load.

reveal.text: Each member's vertical part is its force times rise over length, 1.5/2.5. Two of them hold up 12 kN, so 2F × 1.5/2.5 = 12 and F = 10 kN.

steps.headline: A truss spans 6 m with its apex 4 m high, so each sloping member is 5 m long. A 24 kN load hangs at the apex. Find the force in each sloping member.

workedSteps.text: At the apex two members share the load, each with vertical share rise over length.
Solve for F.
The members push down and outward on the feet, so they are in compression. The bottom member pulls the feet together, so it is in tension.

steps.headline: At joint A of the shallow truss, AC pushes with 10 kN along a line with run 2 m and rise 1.5 m. Find the force in AB.

workedSteps.text: Nothing loads the truss sideways, so the pin at A has no horizontal reaction.
AB must cancel the horizontal part of AC's push: its share is run over length, 2 ÷ 2.5.
Multiply AC's force by that share, in kN.

reveal.text: Think back to the feet: the sloping members push them apart, so AB has to pull them together. A member that pulls on its joints is in tension.

lead.text: Balance the forces on joint D, which carries no load. Members AD and DB lie along one straight line, and DC rises vertically from D to the apex.

reveal.text: You balanced the vertical forces at D: only DC has a vertical part, so it carries none. It is not useless: hang the load from D and it carries it up to the apex.

cases.label: Load at the middle of the tie

lessons.orientation: Find member forces joint by joint and tell tension from compression.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A 12 kN crate rests on two identical vertical posts that share it equally.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the forces in a simple truss one joint at a time, and say whether each member is pulled or pushed.

recap.keyIdea: Isolate one joint with at most two unknown member forces and balance it. Each member is then a pure push or pull along its length.

blocks.text: You found 10 kN in each sloping member of a 4 m truss under 12 kN, and 8 kN pulling along the bottom chord.
You also found that an unloaded joint with two collinear members leaves the third member with no force.

lessons.title: Stress, strain and stiffness

steps.headline: Stress is the force carried by each square millimetre of the cross-section.

lead.text: Stress is internal force per unit area, σ = F/A. Use newtons and square millimetres: 1 N/mm² is 1 MPa. Stress, not force, decides whether a material yields, so a thicker bar carries the same force at lower stress.
Convert the load to newtons first, then divide by the area.

reveal.text: You divided 20,000 N by 400 mm² to get 50 N/mm², which is 50 MPa. A bar of half the area would carry twice that stress.

steps.headline: Strain is the stretch as a fraction of the length, and stress is E times strain.

lead.text: Strain is extension divided by original length, ε = δ/L. It has no unit. In the elastic range, stress and strain are proportional: σ = E × ε. E, Young's modulus, measures stiffness: steel is about 200 GPa, which is 200,000 MPa.

steps.headline: A 3,000 mm steel bar (E = 200 GPa) carries a stress of 60 MPa. How far does it stretch?

workedSteps.text: Write E in MPa so that it matches the unit of stress.
Strain is stress divided by E.
Stretch is strain times the original length.

steps.headline: The bar is 2,000 mm long and its steel has E = 200 GPa. At 50 MPa, how far does it stretch?

workedSteps.text: Write E in MPa.
Strain is stress divided by E.
Multiply the strain by the original length, in mm.

lead.text: Same method, different material. Aluminium is less stiff than steel.

reveal.text: Aluminium has a bit over a third of steel's stiffness, so it stretches nearly three times as much at the same stress and length. Stiffness and strength are different things.

lead.text: Yield stress is where the straight, recoverable part of the stress–strain curve ends. The ultimate strength is the highest stress the bar can hold before it necks and breaks.

reveal.text: 300 MPa is past the 250 MPa yield stress but below the 400 MPa ultimate strength. Unloading removes only the elastic part of the stretch, so a permanent set remains.

lessons.orientation: Relate force per area to stretch per length through Young's modulus.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A 20 kN load hangs from a single steel rod. You replace the rod with two identical rods side by side, sharing the load equally.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn a load into a stress, and a stress into a stretch.

recap.keyIdea: Stress is force over area, and in the elastic range it is E times the strain. Past yield, a bar keeps a permanent stretch.

blocks.text: You turned a 20 kN pull on 400 mm² into 50 MPa, and found that it stretches a 2,000 mm steel bar by 0.5 mm.
The same stress stretches a 1,400 mm aluminium bar by 1 mm, because aluminium is less stiff.

recap.nextHook: A real design never runs a bar at its limit. How much margin is enough?

lessons.title: Factor of safety and sizing

steps.headline: The factor of safety is how many times stronger a member is than its load needs.

lead.text: Engineers compare the stress that would cause failure with the stress the member works at, its working stress. For steel the failure stress is the yield stress.
FoS = yield stress ÷ working stress
The margin covers heavier loads than expected, weaker material, corrosion and errors in the calculation.
Find the working stress first, in MPa. Then compare it with the yield stress.

reveal.text: You found 40,000 N ÷ 400 mm² = 100 MPa, then 250 ÷ 100: the tie works at 40% of its yield stress, a factor of 2.5.

steps.headline: A tie must carry 30 kN with a factor of safety of 2. The steel yields at 250 MPa. Find the least area.

workedSteps.text: Divide the yield stress by the factor to get the allowable stress.
Area is the load in newtons over the allowable stress.

steps.headline: A tie must carry 60 kN with a factor of safety of 2, using steel that yields at 250 MPa. Find the least area.

workedSteps.text: Divide the yield stress by the factor to get the allowable stress.
Divide the load in newtons by the allowable stress, to get the area in mm².

lead.text: Bars come in stock sizes. Choose the smallest one that meets the area you need.

reveal.text: You discarded any bar below the required area, then took the lightest left. Rounding up is normal practice: a larger bar only raises the factor of safety.

lead.text: Strength is not the only check. A member safe against yield may still stretch too much for the connection it serves. Strain is stress ÷ E, with E = 200,000 MPa for steel.

reveal.text: At 96 MPa the tie lengthens 96/200,000 × 3,000 mm. If the connection tolerates only 1 mm, stiffness governs and the section must grow.

lessons.orientation: Size a member for strength with a margin, then check that it is stiff enough.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A lift cable would snap under 100 kN, but it only ever carries 20 kN.

intro.promise: By the end you'll size a steel member from a factor of safety, and check that it does not stretch too much.

recap.keyIdea: The factor of safety is the yield stress divided by the working stress. To size a member, divide the yield stress by the factor to get the allowable stress, then find the area.

blocks.text: You found that 40 kN on 400 mm² gives a factor of safety of 2.5. For 60 kN at a factor of 2 you needed 480 mm², so a 25 mm square bar.
That bar stretches 1.44 mm over 3 m, so stiffness can matter as well as strength.

lessons.title: Shear force and bending moment

steps.headline: The shear force at a cut is the vertical force that holds the left piece still.

lead.text: Imagine sawing a beam in two. Each piece must still balance, so the cut face carries a force: the shear force, V. Add the vertical forces on the left piece, upward positive, to find it. A point load makes the shear jump by its own size.
Cut the beam just to the right of the crate. Both the left reaction and the crate are now on the left piece.

reveal.text: You added the forces on the left piece: 8 kN up and the 12 kN crate down. A point load makes the shear jump by its size, from +8 kN to −4 kN.

steps.headline: The bending moment at a cut is the total moment of the forces on one piece about the cut.

lead.text: The cut face also resists turning. That resistance is the bending moment, M: the moment, about the cut, of all the forces on one piece. Sagging is positive. Use whichever piece has fewer forces; either gives the same size.

steps.headline: A 6 m beam on end supports carries 15 kN at x = 4 m. Find the bending moment under the load.

workedSteps.text: Find the left reaction with moments about B.
Cut under the load. Only RA is to its left, 4 m away.

steps.headline: On the 6 m beam, the 12 kN crate is at x = 2 m and the left reaction is 8 kN. Find the bending moment under the crate.

workedSteps.text: Cut just under the crate. Only the left reaction is on the left piece.
It acts 2 m from the cut. Multiply, in kN·m.

lead.text: By symmetry the peak is at midspan. For a uniform load w over a span L, the standard result for the peak is wL²/8.

reveal.text: Balancing the left half gives the same: 12 kN up at 4 m from the cut, minus 12 kN of load whose centre is 2 m away.

lead.text: The slope of the moment diagram equals the shear force. Move the section marker along the beam and watch both readings.

reveal.text: At the top of the moment curve the slope is level, so the shear there is zero. Find the point where the shear diagram crosses zero and you have found the largest moment.

lessons.orientation: Cut a beam, balance one piece and draw how shear and moment vary along it.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A 6 m plank rests on a post at each end, with a 12 kN crate 2 m from the left end. The left post pushes up with 8 kN.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the shear force and bending moment at any cut along a beam, and say where the moment peaks.

recap.keyIdea: At any cut, the shear force is the sum of the vertical forces on one side and the bending moment is their total moment about the cut. The moment peaks where the shear is zero.

blocks.text: You found a shear force of −4 kN just right of a 12 kN load and a moment of 16 kN·m under it.
Under 3 kN/m on an 8 m beam the moment peaks at 24 kN·m, at midspan, where the shear passes through zero.

lessons.title: Bending stress and the I-beam

steps.headline: Bending stress is zero at the neutral axis and grows with distance from it.

lead.text: Bending stretches one face of a beam and squashes the other. The neutral axis between them carries no stress. Stress grows with distance y from it: σ = My/I. The second moment of area, I, measures how well a section resists bending. For a rectangle, I = bh³/12.
Work in newtons and millimetres: 1 kN·m is 10⁶ N·mm. The largest stress is at the outer fibre.

reveal.text: You found I = 100 × 200³ ÷ 12 = 66.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴. With the outer fibre 100 mm out, σ = 20 × 10⁶ × 100 ÷ 66.7 × 10⁶ = 30 MPa.

steps.headline: A beam 50 mm wide and 120 mm deep carries 6 kN·m. Find the largest bending stress.

workedSteps.text: Find I for the rectangle.
The largest stress is at the outer fibre, half the depth from the axis.
Put the moment in N·mm and use σ = My/I.

steps.headline: The same beam is laid flat, 200 mm wide and 100 mm deep, under the same 20 kN·m. Find the largest bending stress.

workedSteps.text: Swap the width and depth in bh³/12.
The outer fibre is now half of 100 mm from the axis.
Use σ = My/I, with M in N·mm, to get the stress in MPa.

lead.text: Cube the depth before you multiply by the width.

reveal.text: You cubed the depth, 100³, before multiplying by the width. Double the depth and I grows eightfold; that is why joists stand on edge.

lead.text: Material near the neutral axis carries little stress and adds little to I. An I-section moves it into flanges at the top and bottom. Find I as the outer rectangle minus the two empty side regions.

reveal.text: This I-section uses 3,080 mm² against 20,000 mm² for the solid rectangle: 15% of the material, yet it keeps 31% of the I.

lessons.orientation: Use σ = My/I and see why depth and flanges make a beam efficient.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A 100 mm × 200 mm timber plank bridges a gap. You can lay it flat or stand it on its 100 mm edge.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the largest bending stress in a beam, and see why deep sections and I-beams carry bending well.

recap.keyIdea: Bending stress is σ = My/I, largest at the outer fibre. For a rectangle I = bh³/12, so depth matters far more than width.

blocks.text: You found 30 MPa for the plank on edge and 60 MPa laid flat, under the same 20 kN·m.
You also found that an I-section keeps about 31% of the solid rectangle's I with about 15% of its material.

lessons.title: Deflection and stiffness

steps.headline: Tip deflection is the load times the length cubed, over three times EI.

lead.text: A cantilever loaded at its tip bends by δ = PL³/3EI. E and I together, EI, are the flexural rigidity: material stiffness times section shape. Work in base units: newtons, metres, pascals and m⁴. 1 GPa is 10⁹ Pa, and 10⁶ mm⁴ is 10⁻⁶ m⁴.
Convert to base units first. Then find EI, and PL³ divided by three times EI.

reveal.text: You worked in base units: EI = 400,000 N·m² and PL³ = 24,000 N·m³, so δ = 24,000 ÷ 1,200,000 = 0.02 m, which is 20 mm.

steps.headline: A steel cantilever 3 m long (E = 200 GPa, I = 4 × 10⁶ mm⁴) carries 2 kN at its tip. Find the tip deflection.

workedSteps.text: Write E and I in base units.
Work out PL³ in newtons and metres.
Divide by 3EI, then convert to millimetres.

steps.headline: An aluminium cantilever 1 m long (E = 70 GPa, I = 1 × 10⁶ mm⁴) carries 2.1 kN at its tip. Find the tip deflection.

workedSteps.text: Write E and I in base units.
Work out PL³ in newtons and metres.
Divide by 3EI, then convert to millimetres.

lead.text: Only the length changes. Look at where L sits in PL³/3EI.

reveal.text: Length is cubed, so doubling it multiplies the deflection by 2 × 2 × 2. Long spans are often governed by stiffness well before strength.

steps.headline: Stiffness is the load needed for one unit of deflection.

lead.text: Stiffness is load per unit deflection. For an end-loaded cantilever, k = P/δ = 3EI/L³. A diving board is designed for low stiffness; a machine-tool arm needs a very high one.
A machine-tool arm must hold a cutter steady, so engineers ask how much load it takes to move the tip. Use k = 3EI/L³ for the 2 m steel arm.

reveal.text: Each kilonewton at the tip moves this arm about 6.7 mm. Check against the first step: 3 kN ÷ 20 mm gives the same stiffness.

lessons.orientation: Predict how far a cantilever bends with δ = PL³/3EI and trade length, material and shape.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A cantilever carries 3 kN at its tip and sags 20 mm. The material stays elastic.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find how far a cantilever sags under load, and say which change stiffens it most.

recap.keyIdea: A cantilever's tip deflection is PL³/3EI: it grows with the cube of the length and shrinks with EI. Stiffness is the load per unit deflection, 3EI/L³.

blocks.text: You found that a 2 m steel cantilever with 3 kN at its tip sags 20 mm, and 160 mm if it is twice as long.
Its stiffness is 150 kN/m, and 5 × 10⁶ mm⁴ of I keeps it within 8 mm.

lessons.title: Levers and pulleys

steps.headline: A lever trades distance for force: the longer arm needs the smaller force.

lead.text: A lever turns about a fulcrum. The effort you apply and the load you move balance in moments: effort × effort arm = load × load arm. Mechanical advantage is the load divided by the effort. A lever creates no energy.
Balance the moments about the fulcrum. Then compare the load with the effort.

reveal.text: You compared the arms: the effort acts 1.2 m out and the load 0.2 m out. For a balanced lever, MA = effort arm ÷ load arm = 1.2 ÷ 0.2 = 6.

steps.headline: A 2 m bar balances an 800 N load 0.25 m from the fulcrum, with the effort at the far end. Find the effort.

workedSteps.text: Moments about the fulcrum balance.
Work out the load's moment, then divide by the effort arm.

steps.headline: The crowbar's handle is 1.2 m from the fulcrum and the 900 N load is 0.2 m from it. Find the effort.

workedSteps.text: Moments about the fulcrum balance.
Divide by the effort arm, in newtons.

steps.headline: The class of a lever depends on which of the three points is in the middle.

lead.text: A lever has three points: fulcrum, load and effort. First class has the fulcrum in the middle, like a crowbar. Second class has the load in the middle. Third class has the effort in the middle: it gives up force for speed and reach.
In a block and tackle one continuous rope runs over several pulleys. Every strand carries the same tension. Count only the strands attached to, or running round, the moving block.

reveal.text: Four strands share the 800 N, so the rope carries a quarter of it. The more strands, the smaller the effort.

lead.text: An ideal machine returns exactly the work you put in, force × distance. If the effort is smaller, something else must grow. Think about how the rope moves as the block rises.

reveal.text: Each of the 4 strands shortens by 0.5 m, so 2 m of rope passes through your hand. Work in, 200 N × 2 m, equals work out, 800 N × 0.5 m: 400 J both ways.

blocks.text: You found that a crowbar with a 1.2 m handle and a 0.2 m load arm has a mechanical advantage of 6, so it holds 900 N with 150 N.
A 4-strand pulley holds 800 N with 200 N, but you pull 2 m of rope to lift the load 0.5 m.

lessons.title: Gear trains: speed and torque

steps.headline: Meshing gears pass teeth at the same rate, so speed × teeth is equal on both.

lead.text: The driver gear turns the driven gear. Meshing teeth pass the contact point at the same rate, so speed × teeth is the same on both. The gear ratio is driven teeth ÷ driver teeth. A larger gear always turns more slowly.
Speed × teeth is equal on both gears. The larger gear turns more slowly.

reveal.text: You used speed × teeth on both gears: 1,200 × 20 = speed × 60. The 60-tooth gear turns at 20/60 of the driver's speed.

steps.headline: An ideal gear pair passes on all the power, so less speed means more torque.

lead.text: Power is torque times angular speed, and an ideal mesh passes all of it on. Slow the shaft by the gear ratio and its torque rises by the same ratio. A gearbox trades speed for torque, as a lever trades distance for force.

steps.headline: A 24-tooth driver turns at 600 rpm and supplies 8 N·m to a 72-tooth gear. The mesh is lossless. Find the output speed and torque.

workedSteps.text: The gear ratio is driven teeth over driver teeth.
Speed falls by the ratio.
The power is kept, so torque rises by the ratio.

steps.headline: The 20-tooth driver supplies 10 N·m and the mesh is lossless. Find the output torque on the 60-tooth gear.

workedSteps.text: The gear ratio is driven teeth over driver teeth.
Torque rises by the ratio. Multiply the input torque, in N·m.

lead.text: An idler is an extra gear between the driver and the output. It meshes with the driver, so speed × teeth is equal across that mesh. Each external mesh also reverses the direction of rotation.

reveal.text: The idler turns at its own speed, but its teeth cancel from the overall ratio: 1,200 × 20/30 × 30/60 is still 400 rpm for the output.

lead.text: A single pair giving 9 : 1 would need a 135-tooth wheel against a 15-tooth pinion. A compound train fits the same reduction into a smaller box: two gears sit on one shaft, so each stage hands its output speed to the next.

reveal.text: With two gears on a shared shaft, the stage ratios multiply: 45/15 × 60/20 = 3 × 3 = 9, so 1,800 rpm becomes 200 rpm.

lessons.orientation: Use tooth counts to find speed, torque and direction through simple and compound trains.

In a compound train of 3 : 1 stages, 1,800 rpm falls to 200 rpm.

lessons.title: Efficiency and power in a drive

steps.headline: Power is torque times angular speed, with the speed in radians per second.

lead.text: Power is work per second: force × speed along a line, and torque × angular speed in a shaft. For P = Tω, ω must be in radians per second: rpm × 2π ÷ 60. Skip that and the answer is nearly ten times too large.
Convert the speed to radians per second first. Then multiply by the torque.

reveal.text: You converted 1,500 rpm to 157.08 rad/s, then multiplied by 20 N·m to get about 3,142 W. Without the conversion the answer would be almost ten times too large.

steps.headline: A motor delivers 8 N·m at 3,000 rpm. Find its power output.

workedSteps.text: Convert rpm to radians per second.
Multiply torque by angular speed.

steps.headline: Each stage keeps a fraction of the power, and the fractions multiply.

lead.text: Each stage loses some power to friction, and efficiencies multiply: two 90% stages give 0.9 × 0.9 = 81%. Teeth cannot slip, so losses show up as lost torque, not lost speed. Friction also raises the effort a machine needs: its real mechanical advantage is the ideal one × efficiency.

steps.headline: A gearbox has two meshes, each 95% efficient. Find the overall efficiency.

workedSteps.text: Each mesh passes on 0.95 of the power it receives.
Multiply the two efficiencies, then give the answer as a percentage.

lead.text: Teeth cannot slip, so a 4 : 1 gearbox still turns at exactly a quarter of the input speed. The missing power shows up as lost torque.

reveal.text: The ideal output would be 20 × 4 = 80 N·m. At 90% efficiency the shaft delivers 72 N·m, with the speed unchanged.

lead.text: Size a motor from the useful output. Power at the hook is force × speed. The motor supplies that plus whatever is lost on the way.

reveal.text: Lifting 2,000 N at 0.5 m/s needs 1,000 W at the hook. At 80% efficiency the motor must supply 1,250 W.

lessons.orientation: Track power through a drive, account for losses and size a motor for a hoist.

blocks.text: You found 3,142 W for 20 N·m at 1,500 rpm, and that two 95% meshes deliver 90.25% of the power.
